document.title: The Ferry Ledger
document.text:
The Ferry Ledger

On the morning the ferry stopped coming, Mara found a brass key in the till. It lay beneath the roll of unused tickets, warm enough that she first thought someone had just put it there. The office had been locked since six the previous evening. Above the till, the clock made its usual patient corrections to the silence.

She set the key beside the ledger and counted the money. Twelve pounds in coins, a torn five-pound note, a washer that had passed for a shilling before the currency changed. The washer was her father's joke. She left it in the drawer because removing it seemed a larger act than leaving it there.

Outside, three people waited on the slip. Mr Vale held a parcel against his coat. The woman who cleaned the island school had a string bag and no gloves. A boy in the uniform of the mainland college stood apart from them, looking at his phone as though the weather were a service it had failed to provide. The mist obscured the far bank. It did not obscure the absence of an engine.

Mara opened the hatch.

"They'll have rung," Mr Vale said.

"Not here."

He looked at the telephone on the desk. She picked it up for him, listened to the empty connection, and put it down. Across the water a bell struck once, without deciding to go on.

The woman with the string bag said she would wait until half past. The boy said nothing. Mr Vale asked if the road round was still open, and Mara told him it was, although the road was twenty miles and he had never learned to drive. People asked her questions to which the answer changed nothing. Her father had said that was half the job.

After half past, the woman left. The boy stayed until a van came for him. Mr Vale moved from the slip to the bench outside the office, where he set the parcel on his knees and watched the hatch. Mara pretended to work on the ledger. The last entry was in her father's writing. He had taken the Wednesday shift for her in March, three days before he died, and she had not been able to write below it. Instead she kept the subsequent fares on sheets of paper which she folded into the cover.

At ten she made tea in two chipped cups. Mr Vale accepted his through the hatch. The parcel was wrapped in brown paper which had been carefully saved from something else; old creases crossed the new ones. There was no address.

"Is that for somebody on the island?"

"For the house," he said.

There was only one house on the island which people called the house. Its owner had gone away in winter. The shutters were green, though from the mainland they looked black. Mara had once delivered a crate of bottles there with her father. She remembered the kitchen table and a bowl of apricots, and a woman holding a glass too close to its rim. It had seemed improbable to her then that anyone who lived on an island would choose not to have a view of the water from the kitchen.

"Nobody's there," Mara said.

"I know."

He drank the tea standing up. She thought he might explain himself, but he returned the empty cup and went back to the bench. She did not ask again. In the office there were several things which demanded a question: the new key, the dead telephone, the ledger she would not finish. A parcel could wait its turn.

By eleven the mist had thinned. The ferry's berth on the far side was empty. Nothing moved at the boatyard except a sheet hung between two posts. She tried the company's number from her own phone. After a long interval a recorded voice told her to visit a website. On the website, under a photograph of a vessel they had never used on this crossing, a green light announced that all services were operating normally.

She wrote OUT OF SERVICE on a ticket and pushed it into the hatch's little metal frame. The words were too large; SERVICE bent at the edge. Then she took it out again. She knew no more than the three people who had waited at the slip. Writing down a conclusion did not make it knowledge.

The key had a flattened bow and two uneven teeth. It was not for the office or the storage shed. Mara carried it to the door and tried it in the lock anyway. The wrongness of the fit was reassuring. At least that was settled. She could put it in an envelope marked FOUND, as her father had done with watches, school passes, a wedding ring. The drawer below the till still held the envelopes. Some of them had outlasted the people who had lost their contents.

Under the wedding ring she found a map of the harbor. It was a map meant for work, not visitors. No lighthouse, no little waves: depths in pencil, a cross where the old landing had been, a line showing the water main which had never been laid. Her father had marked an inland path with a red arrow. The arrow led from the island slip to a square behind the house, a building Mara did not remember seeing.

She held the key over the square, absurdly, as if one might unlock the other. Then she folded the map and put it back.

At noon a car stopped at the gate. The driver did not get out. He lowered his window far enough to ask about the ferry, and when she said she was still waiting to hear, he raised it and reversed into the road. The engine's departure left Mr Vale looking smaller on the bench. Mara wanted him to complain. A complaint would have given her something familiar to do.

"I'm going to close for lunch," she told him.

"Of course."

"You can leave that here if you'd rather not carry it."

He looked at the parcel, then at her, then back at the water. His hand moved under the paper as though to check that it was still holding.

"I ought to take it myself."

"When there's a boat."

"Yes. When there's a boat."

She shut the hatch but left the door open. Her sandwich had gone soft at the corners. She ate standing beside the desk. Beyond the doorway Mr Vale unwrapped the parcel. There was a length of pale cloth inside, folded around something rigid. For a moment she thought it was a book. He laid the cloth across his knees. The thing beneath it was a wooden frame with no picture in it.

He turned the frame over, smoothing the cloth into each empty corner. Mara could see that his movements were not quite practical. They belonged to some older task for which this was an imperfect substitute. Her father had done that after her mother left: set three plates out, then return one to the cupboard as if correcting an oversight. Nobody had asked him to stop.

The office telephone rang.

Mara swallowed before lifting the receiver. The first sound was wind. Then a man said her name. He sounded close enough that she looked out at the slip, expecting someone with a phone held to his ear. There was only Mr Vale, the frame, and the water settling around the pilings.

"Mara? It's Owen. I've got the ferry at the yard."

Owen had taken over after her father. He was competent with machinery and uncomfortable with people. In four months he had never called her by name. She waited for the explanation to come in the familiar order: an apology, a part, a time.

"She's not broken," he said. "I need you to understand that first."

Mara sat down. The key made a small bright sound when her sleeve caught it and sent it against the ledger. Owen stopped speaking. She could hear his breath, and beneath it the faint scrape of something being dragged along wood.

"What is it, then?"

"Your father left something on board. I didn't know what to do with it."

Outside, Mr Vale had risen from the bench. He was standing in the doorway now, holding the empty frame against his chest. Mara kept the receiver to her ear and

examples.title: The baker
examples.text: The baker left the back door open because the heat had nowhere else to go. At four in the morning a fox stood in the doorway. It did not enter. Flour whitened the tiles, and the oven clicked behind him with the small, domestic noise of something cooling. He broke the heel from yesterday's loaf and set it on the step. By the time he looked again, both the bread and the fox were gone. A single paw print remained on the flour. He swept around it until daylight.

examples.title: The parked car
examples.text:
"Have you told her?"

"I wrote a letter."

"That isn't what I asked."

They were sitting in the car with the engine off. Rain gathered on the windshield, and every few minutes a drop found the route made by the one before it. He watched this happen several times before he answered.

"I thought if I wrote it down, I could get the words right."

She put her hand on the door handle, but did not open the door.

"There isn't a right order. There is only an order in which she hears it."
